name: Well travelled road effect
statement: Routes a traveller knows well are judged to take less time than unfamiliar routes of the same length.
meaning: The claim runs two measurements together. One is the estimate given before setting out, the time a person says a walk or drive to a known place will take. The other is how long a journey is remembered as having taken once it is over. The proposed mechanism is attentional. A familiar route is driven or walked with little conscious control, fewer events are laid down, and the interval is reconstructed as short. That mechanism is borrowed from the general literature on duration judgement, where manipulating routine shortens remembered duration. Whether it produces the particular effect this name describes is a separate question. The name itself did not come from a laboratory. It was coined in a Wikipedia article, and a systematic review of the route-familiarity literature located a single study that measured the claim.

Another editor added notability and referencing tags within six minutes, at 07:12 UTC. On 8 April 2026 the same account added the words 'coined by Jeffrey Popova-Clark in 2010', and on 9 April 2026 it cited the page's own revision history for them.

evidence: Anna Jafarpour and Hugo Spiers ran the one study that measures the claim directly. They tested 20 international students, 13 men and 7 women, mean age 27 with SD 3, who had lived nine months at William Goodenough House in Bloomsbury with no prior knowledge of the area and had travelled it on foot only. Each drew a south-up sketch map of the district, then estimated in minutes the walk to each of 19 destinations within about a mile, then marked the two to five routes they took daily. Two participants were dropped, leaving 18. Paths lying on the daily routes were classed as highly familiar. Both sets of paths were drawn longer than the probe scale, the highly familiar at 3.15 with SD 1.55 and the less familiar at 2.26 with SD 1.39, and the difference between them was reliable, t(17) = 2.975, P = 0.0085. Destinations were then matched within each participant for distance, after which the two sets did not differ in path distance, t(17) = 0.53, P = 0.60, in straight-line distance, t(17) = 1.3, P = 0.21, or in number of turns, t(17) = 0.43, P = 0.66. Estimated arrival time for highly familiar destinations was shorter than for less-familiar ones, t(17) = 2.17, P = 0.044. Measured against walking times from Google Maps, estimates for highly familiar destinations ran 1.5 minutes short with SD 2.69, and less-familiar ones 0.1 minutes short with SD 3.22. The authors had predicted the opposite direction from rodent grid-cell data and report that they found the opposite of their prediction. Familiarity was observed rather than assigned: participants nominated their own daily routes. The references the Wikipedia article now carries do not test the claim. Its only original reference, Jackson and Jucker, put hypothetical commutes to respondents and fitted each person's willingness to trade mean travel time against travel time variability. Its abstract describes no measurement of familiarity. Zakay and Block report two experiments on prospective and retrospective duration reproductions under executive load, one on resolving syntactic ambiguity while reading and one on task switching with 96 students. Rubia and Smith review functional imaging of motor timing and time estimation. The words route, travel and navigation appear nowhere in either paper.

examples.tag: Two walks of the same length
examples.text: The daily walk to the office is put at ten minutes and an unfamiliar walk to a dentist the same distance away at twenty. Both take the same time, and the only thing separating the estimates is how often one of them has been made.

A driver reaches work unable to name a single junction passed, and says the trip went quickly. The route was driven with little attention, so few events were laid down for the mind to count back over when it judged the interval.

examples.tag: The school run in a new town
examples.text: After a family moves, the drive to the new school feels long for the first fortnight and shortens as the turns become automatic. The clock records the same minutes throughout, and what changes is the familiarity of the road.

replication.headline: No repeat of the single 20-person study was found. A systematic review of 94 route-familiarity studies rated the travel time finding at its weakest evidence grade, meaning one paper.
replication.detail: Ilse Harms, Bridget Burdett and Samuel Charlton searched Scopus under PRISMA and screened 1228 records, removing 259 duplicates and adding 11 from their own knowledge. Of 980 records, 857 were excluded on title and abstract, 123 were read in full and 29 dropped, leaving 94 eligible articles. Seven of those addressed spatial and temporal memory. Two reported memory accuracy falling with familiarity, both on walking, and both found that pedestrians drew or judged highly familiar paths as longer in distance. Those two are Jafarpour and Spiers and Crompton's Manchester study. One of the two also measured time, and reported travel time underestimated with practice. That one is Jafarpour and Spiers. The review's rating scheme sets 'an indication' at one paper comparing familiar with unfamiliar conditions, which is what this finding received. The space and time dissociation itself has been produced again with a different manipulation, in the same laboratory. Iva Brunec, Amir-Homayoun Javadi, Fiona Zisch and Spiers had participants estimate travel time and straight-line distance to learned destinations in a virtual town, comparing roughly linear routes with routes needing circumnavigation. Travel times were underestimated and straight-line distances overestimated for all routes, and both biases grew where the route had to be navigated around an obstacle. Familiarity was not the variable. Transport research that did compare perceived travel times by familiarity points the other way. Jaap Vreeswijk, Tom Thomas, Eric van Berkum and Bart van Arem recruited drivers at car parks on the university campus in Enschede and put four route pairs in the city to them, giving 624 valid choices. Travel times were overestimated in general, and the perceived travel times of the least familiar respondents were shorter than those of the most familiar, statistically significant at 95% for two of the four routes and for the average. Estimates from the least familiar respondents were among the most accurate; those from the most familiar sat near the busiest and highest recorded peak times.

limits: The verdict covers the claim that route familiarity shortens travel time judgements. It does not cover the wider finding that routine shortens remembered duration, which rests on a much larger literature and is treated in the time-perception entry. The evidence base is one observational study of 18 analysed participants in one square mile of London, on foot, with self-nominated familiar routes and Google Maps as the standard of truth. No effect size is reported for the time comparison, so the structured fields are empty. This is also a one-laboratory literature. Jafarpour and Spiers, and the circumnavigation study that produced the space and time dissociation again, both come from Hugo Spiers's group at University College London. No test of the travel time claim by anyone outside that group was located. The search ran on 21 September 2026 across Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed, OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar. It also covered the Harms review's own 94-study appendix and the 25 records Europe PMC holds as citing Jafarpour and Spiers, two of them preprint versions of articles already in that list. None of the 25 repeats the familiarity manipulation on travel time. Vreeswijk and colleagues' figures are read from the first author's doctoral thesis at the University of Twente. That thesis carries the paper as chapter 6 and names the journal version on the chapter's first page. The two were not compared, because Unpaywall and OpenAlex both record the journal version as closed. Three documents could not be obtained on 21 September 2026. Allan's 1979 review is listed by Unpaywall as free at the publisher, and link.springer.com answers this session with a JavaScript client challenge rather than a paywall, so it is unread and nothing is said here about what is in it. Zakay and Fallach's 1984 comparison is closed at Elsevier and its PubMed record carries no abstract; what it contains is known here only through Zakay and Block's description of it. Jackson and Jucker's full text sits behind a bot challenge at pubsonline.informs.org and a captcha at RePEc, so only the abstract at Crossref was read. Whether the effect exists for drivers, which is the case the popular description leads with, was not established: the one study tested pedestrians.
misreadings: The effect is routinely merged with the return trip effect, and the two disagree about the cause. Niels van de Ven, Leon van Rijswijk and Michael Roy found the return trip seeming shorter on a bus trip, a bicycle trip and a video of somebody else travelling, and they found it again when an equidistant but different route was taken home. They state the conclusion plainly: it is not familiarity with the route that causes the effect, and a violation of expectations appears to. In their bus study, how many waypoints travellers recognised was unrelated to the effect, beta = .15, t(67) = 1.21, p = .23. Jafarpour and Spiers cite that paper, along with two other return trip studies, as prior reports of familiarity shortening travel time. Ryosuke Ozawa, Keisuke Fujii and Motoki Kouzaki narrowed it further. Twenty men watched walking-route films, ten in a round trip and ten not. On an unannounced eleven-point comparison afterwards the round trip group rated the second leg shorter than zero, t(9) = -6.53, p = 0.00011, and every one of the ten gave a negative score. The control group did not differ from zero, t(9) = 0.60, p = .57. Between groups the difference gave t(12) = -2.92, p = .013, d = -1.31. On repeated production of three-minute intervals during the films, made in real time, the group by session interaction was absent, F(1,18) = 0.84, p = .37, partial eta squared .04. The effect showed up after the journey and not during it. The second error is extending 'familiar routes feel shorter' to distance. Both studies that measured distance found the reverse. Jafarpour and Spiers' participants drew their most familiar paths longest. Andrew Crompton asked Manchester architecture students to estimate walking distances to 22 destinations along Oxford Road, and analysed the 140 forms that came back with three or fewer entries missing, having set aside 45 first-year forms and two third-year ones. A Manchester mile came out at 1.24 miles for a first year who had been there two months, 1.33 for a second year at 14 months and 1.45 for a third year at 26 months. Crompton prints no significance test for that rise, and writes that it must be judged from the graphs. Kyung Wook Seo, Hyung-Sook Lee and Joo Young Kim ran a similar design on two campus routes in Suwon and found estimates shrinking rather than growing across year groups, and say in the paper that this is the opposite of Crompton's result. The mechanism is also stated with more confidence than anything supports. The Wikipedia article compares the effect to the Stroop task and hangs that comparison on Zakay and Fallach's 1984 paper, which Zakay and Block describe as varying the difficulty of a Stroop task rather than the familiarity of a route. Popular retellings tend to be sourced to a different finding again. PsyBlog's article on the well-travelled road effect cites Avni-Babad and Ritov's work on routine and the perception of time. They established routine through markers, task variation and repeated blocks, and through field studies of vacationers and kibbutz members, not through route familiarity.

sources.text: Wikipedia, 'Well travelled road effect'. The article, its current wikitext, the first revisions and the full revision list were read through the MediaWiki API on 21 September 2026. Source for the coinage, the creation date and time, the account Jeffpc2, the original single reference, the notability and referencing tags within six minutes, and the April 2026 self-attribution.

Harms, I. M., Burdett, B. R. D., & Charlton, S. G. (2021). The role of route familiarity in traffic participants' behaviour and transport psychology research: A systematic review. Transportation Research Interdisciplinary Perspectives, 9, 100331. Read in full from the University of Groningen repository copy; the source for the 94 studies, the screening counts, the evidence rating scheme and the identity of the two memory studies.
